input.question: Why does pinching a hose at its extremity make the water flow faster while pinching in the middle make the water flow weaker?
input.ground_truth: because it reduces the volume moving past that point while increasing the speed due to the pressure behind. When you pinch in the middle, the volume is restricted, but then expanded again, meaning the rest of the hose has reduced pressure and volume, due to the expanded area. If you keep the hose pinched all the way along from the first pinch point to the end, the water will flow faster (but you'll have increased friction all along that stretch which will slow things down a bit).

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: Why does pinching a hose at its extremity make the water flow faster while pinching in the middle make the water flow weaker?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have a big, soft straw (that's your hose) and you're blowing water through it. 

If you pinch the very end of the straw (the **extremity**), the water can only come out of a tiny opening. It has to squeeze through that little spot, so it comes out **really fast**, like when you squeeze a toothpaste tube.

But if you pinch the middle of the straw, you make the whole tube smaller in the middle. Now, the water can't get through that pinched part easily, so it doesn't come out as fast, or maybe it stops coming out at all, like when you squeeze a balloon in the middle and it gets hard to blow air through.

So, pinching the end makes the water go **faster**, and pinching the middle makes the water go **slower or stop**!
